prize_parts.citation: For showing how borrowing limits tied to collateral values amplify and propagate shocks, and for establishing a dynamic theory of credit cycles.

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged: B007 with Kiyotaki and Moore. The discovery is a specific dynamic mechanism. Borrowing limits tied to collateral values feed back on asset prices, so temporary shocks become persistent and amplified. It is a conceptual result, not a tool or an estimation method. It is roughly three decades old, so the Committee is not judging it early. It became the base for later work on financial frictions, intermediary balance sheets and macroprudential analysis, and it shaped how the 2008 crisis was understood. The credit rests on one two-author paper, and I can state that cleanly without a contested cut. I treat that cleanliness as a property of the attribution, not as extra merit. On merit alone I regard B007, B026 and B012 as close. B007 is narrower than B012 in policy footprint. I judge it a more durable and more precisely identified discovery than a prize that would require a contestable three-name cut from eight credited names. The round-1 exchange did not change my ranking of the three. It did change my view of how to answer the chair's question on the 2022 prize. Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig recognised bank runs, deposit insurance and the role of bank failures in the Great Depression. Kiyotaki-Moore is an amplification mechanism through collateral and asset prices, and it needs no run or intermediary failure. I would still want the citation to state that distinction explicitly.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises is the main reservation, since a Committee could read Kiyotaki-Moore as a refinement of recognised ground. A second reservation is that the mechanism is better established in theory and quantitative models than through clean identification of collateral channels. Several colleagues made this point, and I accept it. Breadth also counts against B007. It has less reach than the New Keynesian framework in B012 and less reach across applied fields than firm heterogeneity in B026. The pair also leaves out Gertler and Gilchrist, whose accelerator and intermediary-friction work was influential. I judge that a separable strand, but the omission is a cost. I have no majority on this configuration and I do not treat that as evidence on merit. B026 has repeated firm-level confirmation, and a Melitz-Helpman pair could be defended if the Committee accepts its attribution boundaries.

responses.point: Strömberg proposes a two-part prize: Kiyotaki and Moore for B007 and Melitz alone for B026. He concedes that the one-person B026 part may reflect the three-person cap and that he would rather name Helpman.
responses.response: I considered the combination, because it would join two of the three groups of preferring members. I do not support it. Under the three-person cap it forces Melitz to stand alone, and Strömberg himself says this looks like a product of the cap. The two achievements are also unrelated. A prize in macro-finance and a prize in trade theory gain nothing from being joined, and the pairing would split the credit instead of improving it. If the Committee prefers B026, the right form is Melitz and Helpman together as a single part, and I would not oppose that. I would keep B007 as its own prize, with Kiyotaki and Moore, as the cleaner statement of what is being honoured.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, prefers B012 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford and ranks B007 second. He concedes that the Taylor rule is closer to a rule of thumb than a deep theorem. He says the strongest alternatives, B007 and B026, have cleaner two-name attribution.
responses.response: We agree on the substance of B007: the Kiyotaki-Moore pair is a well-defined discovery. My disagreement is about what the diffuse credit in B012 implies. I accept that Calvo and Woodford are strong originators, but Taylor's claim rests on staggered contracts, with the rule as the policy-facing part. If Gali would replace Taylor, as three B012 supporters now say, the trio is not stable. A prize whose composition depends on that judgment is less ready than one with a stable pair, even though its policy influence is larger. I do not say B012 is weaker as science. I say the Committee has not yet shown which three strands it is honouring. Hassler also asked whether I would add Gertler. I would not, for the reasons given in my round-1 file: his credit competes with B012 and overlaps the Bernanke-linked accelerator. I also disclose that Hassler is my frequent co-author, so he and I may share a prior on this field that others do not.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B012 first. He says B007 has the cleaner two-person attribution but a narrower mechanism, and he ranks it lower on scope. He treats diffuse credit as no reason to rank B012 below B007.
responses.response: His scope point is fair, and I concede that B012's footprint in policy practice is larger than B007's. We differ on how to weigh that against attribution. Scope tells me how much the work matters. It does not tell me which people deserve credit for it. A broad framework with eight claimants and a contested three-person cut puts the Committee's own judgment into the prize in a way a two-author mechanism does not. I also accept his point that the Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans line is a separate achievement and should not be folded into B012 under the cap. That strengthens my view that B012's credit boundary is the hard problem. On scope I would say only that the amplification logic of B007 is used in models well beyond monetary policy, but I have not independently verified the breadth of that use.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B026 first with Melitz and Helpman. She gives repeated firm-level testing as a reason to prefer it. She notes that identification of collateral channels is less clean than the Kiyotaki-Moore theory and that the 2022 prize partly covers the ground.
responses.response: I agree on the identification gap and I have not dismissed it. Collateral channels are harder to isolate than the exporter-selection facts in customs data, and B026 has the stronger record of direct testing. We differ on how much weight that should carry. A discovery's value lies in the mechanism the field now reasons with, as well as in a decisive test, and I think post-2008 work shows that for Kiyotaki-Moore. The uncertainty about attribution at the edges of B026 is what keeps it as my first alternative, not my preferred part. The question for the Committee is whether Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, who are outside this ballot entry, are such serious omissions that a Melitz-Helpman pair is premature. I do not think that question is closed. If colleagues judge that Melitz's originating role settles it, I would regard B026 as a strong prize, and I would not rank it far below B007 on merit.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats Kiyotaki-Moore as distinct from the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, or reads it as a refinement of recognised ground.
How securely the collateral channel is identified empirically compared with the theory and the quantitative models.
Whether B026 should rank above B007 on merit once the repeated firm-level testing is weighed against the uncredited Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum lines.
Whether the Committee can settle B012's credit boundary, and whether the 2021-23 inflation should move the assessment of that framework.
I have not independently verified citation counts, priority claims or the empirical literature beyond the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: From my profile: I am the committee secretary and a frequent co-author of Timo Boppart (co-opted member) and John Hassler (chair). Both are IIES colleagues. Boppart also prefers B007, and Hassler prefers B012 and ranks B007 second, so my views overlap with theirs and I disclose this without adjudicating it. I have co-authored with Anthony Smith, Ríos-Rull, Violante, Greenwood, Hercowitz, Tsyvinski and Olovsson, none of whom is credited on B007, B026 or B012. My field of macroeconomic theory is adjacent to B007 and B012. The profile shows no personal or institutional connection to Kiyotaki, Moore, Melitz or Helpman, nor to Calvo, Taylor, Woodford or Gertler. This is unchanged from round 1.
